I have, once. It was a long eighteen months, but we kept the clients, and that was the part the buyer paid for.

I would, if the board was clear about the timetable. Is a sale on the table here?

When I give feedback to a candidate after a first round, the most common note is the same: your answers were right, but they were long. Senior people over-explain because they have prepared so much, and they want to use all of it. So when the panel asks a yes or no question, they repeat the whole question back, add the context, and then the answer arrives at the end. In the second round, I tell them to try something simple. If the question is have you done this, start with I have, or I haven't. Then give one fact, and stop. It feels too short to them. To the panel, it sounds like somebody who is sure of the answer.

I have interviewed a lot of finance directors whose English was better than mine, and some of them still sounded stilted. They spoke in complete paragraphs. If I asked whether they would relocate, I got a speech about family and career. The candidate I hired last year did something different. I asked if he expected the market to recover, and he said, I think so, but not before the autumn. I asked if he had ever lost a client, and he said, I have, and I would rather tell you how we won the next one. It was a real back-and-forth. I stopped interviewing him and started talking to him, and that is usually the moment I decide.

Joanna asks if he found the office all right, and he says he did. She asks if he has ever run finance for a business that was being sold, and he says he has, once. He says he would do it again, if the board was clear about the timetable. She asks if the team is strong enough, and he says he thinks so. Finally, he mentions one small concern: the reporting line.
